analytic.title: Cost of Robustness of independent WCRT analysis for CBS of Ethernet AVB using eligible intervals

div.p: The existing worst-case response time (WCRT) analysis for individual priority classes under credit-based shaping (CBS) in Ethernet AVB based on so-called eligible intervals is both independent and tight. This WCRT analysis does not rely on any assumptions on interfering inter-priority streams other than those enforced by the Ethernet standard. A major advantage of this independent analysis is that CBS may be viewed as resource reservation, where allocated bandwidth is both guaranteed and enforced. Although independent analysis provides inter-priority class robustness, it comes at a cost of overprovisioning bandwidth. We illustrate this cost of inter-priority class robustness by means of an example that requires 7.8 times the amount of bandwidth reservation for a given set of streams compared to a different analysis that takes knowledge of interpriority streams into account.

div.head: A. Background and motivation
div.p: In the high-tech and automotive industry, there is a need for high bandwidth communication combined with the possibility to give real-time guarantees through a widely accepted standard. Since the development of the Ethernet AVB standard by the Audio/Video Bridging Task group 1 , Ethernet became a viable solution to this problem. To be able to guarantee upper bounds on latencies and required throughput, this standard introduced credit-based shaping (CBS) [1] for two traffic classes, i.e. the Stream Reservation (SR) classes A and B . This key flow control approach shapes the outgoing traffic of a switch based on priority levels and credit levels.

Today, a variety of worst-case response time (WCRT) analysis techniques exist for individual messages under CBS [2]- [8]. As illustrated in [9], which presents an efficient analysis of bandwidth reservation for CBS, an analysis based on socalled eligible intervals [4] typically outperforms an analysis based on busy periods, such as [5], for classes A and B . Moreover, the analysis in [4] does not rely on any assumptions on interfering inter-priority streams other than those enforced by the Ethernet standard [10], i.e. it is independent of arrival patterns and transmission times of packets of those streams, whereas other existing analysis does rely on assumptions on This work has been performed in the context of the PENTA Call 3 project 17006 HiPer (High Performance Vehicle Computer and Communication System for Autonomous Driving). 1 The AVB Task Group was renamed to Time-Sensitive Networking (TSN) Task Group in November 2012.

interfering inter-priority streams. Despite of the fact that the analysis is independent, it is tight, even when the analysis is extended to more than two priority classes [6]. Independence of the analysis has as an additional and major advantage that CBS may be viewed as resource reservation [11], where allocated bandwidth to a priority class is both guaranteed and enforced. Finally, that analysis is considerably simpler and has a linear (instead of a pseudo-polynomial) complexity.

div.head: B. Problem description
div.p: By assuming specific tighter bounds on the worst-case transmission times of packets of interfering inter-priority streams, the analysis can be improved, i.e. lower values might be found for worst-case response times of packets or bandwidth reservations for priority classes. As a result, a system with given bandwidth reservations may be deemed schedulable for these specific bounds, whereas the same system may not be schedulable for worst-case transmission times of packets of inter-priority streams based on the maximum frame size of the Ethernet standard [10]. Similarly, the bandwidth reservations required for a system for these specific bounds may be significantly smaller than those required when worst-case transmission times of packets of inter-priority streams are assumed based on the standard.

Obviously, basing the WCRT analysis on assumptions about the transmission times of packets of interfering inter-priority streams gives rise to robustness concerns, i.e. a system may miss deadlines when these assumptions do not hold. In this paper, we are particularly interested in the so-called cost of robustness, i.e. the additional bandwidth requirements resulting from the independence of the analysis. This paper presents inter-priority class robustness as a binary property, i.e. bandwidth reservations are either robust or not robust. Alternative approaches are conceivable, see e.g. [12] for a definition of a robustness metric for resource allocation, but fall outside of the scope of this paper.

div.head: C. Contributions
div.p: In this paper, we present a simple, albeit extreme, example illustrating that independent analysis may require 7.8 times the amount of bandwidth reservation for a given set of streams compared to analysis that takes knowledge of inter-priority streams into account.

div.head: D. Organization
div.p: The remainder of this note has the following structure. In Section II, we present the bare essentials of the model. Section III presents a recap of bandwidth reservation for CBS, based on [9]. The extreme example is the topic of Section IV. A directions for future work is discussed in Section V. This paper is concluded in Section VI.

div.head: II. REAL-TIME SYSTEM MODEL
div.p: In this section, we model the behavior at the output port of a single switch that is part of an Ethernet AVB network, with a focus on CBS [13] and using the notation of [9].

As a basis, Ethernet AVB adopts non-preemptive strict priority scheduling, where frames of the same priority class are treated in a first-in-first-out (FIFO) manner. On top of this, Ethernet AVB adds a CBS mechanism for the (highest) priority classes to limit traffic bursts. Credit for a priority class X under CBS starts at 0 (zero). A frame of X can only start its transmission if X has non-negative credit. While a frame is transmitted, the credit drops at a rate of α - X . If credit is negative, no further frames can be transmitted and credit rises with a rate of α + X . Credit also rises at a rate of α + X if X has pending frames but cannot transmit. Positive credit is reset to 0 if X has no pending frames. In this paper, we assume a totally ordered set of (only) three priority classes, i.e. A, B , and BE ; see also Figure 1, where A, B , and BE are denoted by H , M , and L, respectively. Priority class H has highest and L has lowest priority. Only classes H and M are subject to bandwidth reservation. We make the following assumptions for the classes H and M , where BW represents the total bandwidth

For the analysis, we assume a physical-layer interpretation (rather than a linklayer interpretation [15]) of the Ethernet standard. div.head: IV. AN EXTREME EXAMPLE
div.p: In this section, we first present an example, and subsequently look at both a robust and a non-robust bandwidth reservation for the example. The robust bandwidth reservation is based on independent analysis, i.e. makes no assumptions about inter-priority streams other than those enforced by the Ethernet standard [13]. The non-robust bandwidth reservation is based on knowledge of the inter-priority streams. The section is concluded with the cost of robustness for the example.

div.head: D. Cost of Robustness
div.p: We present two metrics to express the cost of robustness. The first metric F CoR is the ratio of the robust bandwidth reservation and the non-robust bandwidth reservation:
div.formula: F CoR = α +,R H + α +,R M α +,NR H + α +,NR M .
div.p: For our example, F CoR = 1 0.128 ≈ 7.8. The second metric CoR expresses the cost of robustness as the relative increase of the bandwidth reservation:
div.formula: CoR = (α +,R H + α +,R M ) -(α +,NR H + α +,NR M ) (α +,NR H + α +,NR M ) × 100%.(2)
div.p: For our example, we find CoR = 1-0.128 0.128 × 100% = 681.3%. These metrics indicate significant cost of robustness for the example presented.

div.head: V. DISCUSSION
div.p: Independent (yet tight) WCRT has, as a major advantage, that CBS may be viewed as resource reservation, albeit at potentially a high cost. We therefore aim at investigating mechanisms complementing TSN to enhance CBS towards cost-effective reservations. An example of such a mechanism is unconditional frame skipping of frames that are too large, as supported by the 'Per-stream filtering and policing' mechanisms described in [13]. However, frame filtering and policing is only viable for cases where loss of individual frames is not problematic, e.g. for the best-effort class BE , in general, skipping frames should remain a last resort, in particular for frames of streams of priority classes under CBS. More robust alternatives, albeit with acceptable cost, should thus be investigated.

div.head: VI. CONCLUSION
div.p: We presented a simple, yet extreme, example illustrating the cost of robustness of independent WCRT analysis for CBS of Ethernet AVB using eligible intervals. The example has a utilization of approximately 0.128, and requires the entire bandwidth for a bandwidth reservation based on independent analysis. Based on the example, we conclude that the cost of inter-priority class robustness, expressed in terms of additional bandwidth reservation for classes H and M , may be as large as a factor 7.8, i.e. an increase of approximately 681%! As future work, we aim at invesitgating an alternative metric for robustness [12] and mechanisms complementing TSN to enhance CBS towards cost-effective reservations.
